title: Verifying Ohm's Law
summary: Measure voltage and current across a resistor to verify that V = IR.
theory: Ohm's Law states that the current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points, provided temperature stays constant. Mathematically, **V = IR**, where V is voltage (volts), I is current (amperes), and R is resistance (ohms). The constant of proportionality, R, is a property of the conductor itself.

procedure.title: Build the circuit
procedure.description: Connect a resistor, ammeter, and voltmeter in the simulated circuit as shown.

procedure.title: Vary the supply voltage
procedure.description: Increase the source voltage in five equal steps, recording the ammeter reading at each step.

procedure.title: Tabulate results
procedure.description: Record each (V, I) pair in the observation table provided by the simulation.

procedure.title: Plot V vs I
procedure.description: Plot voltage against current; the slope of the resulting straight line is the resistance.

observation: The V-I graph should be a straight line through the origin. The slope (V/I) should match the labelled resistance value within experimental error.

quiz.question: According to Ohm's Law, if voltage doubles while resistance stays constant, current will:
quiz.explanation: Since I = V/R, doubling V with R constant doubles I.

quiz.question: What does the slope of a V-I graph represent?
quiz.explanation: Slope = ΔV/ΔI = R by definition of Ohm's Law.

title: Series and Parallel Resistor Networks
summary: Compare equivalent resistance and current distribution in series versus parallel circuits.
theory: In a **series** circuit, resistors share the same current and total resistance is the sum of individual resistances (R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...). In a **parallel** circuit, resistors share the same voltage and the reciprocal of total resistance is the sum of reciprocals (1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...).

procedure.title: Build a series circuit
procedure.description: Connect three resistors end-to-end with a single ammeter and measure total current.

procedure.title: Build a parallel circuit
procedure.description: Reconnect the same resistors in parallel and measure the current through each branch.

procedure.title: Compare equivalent resistance
procedure.description: Calculate R_eq for both configurations and compare with the simulation's multimeter reading.

observation: Series current is identical through every component; parallel branch currents sum to the total supply current, and parallel R_eq is always less than the smallest branch resistance.

quiz.question: Adding another resistor in parallel to an existing network will:
quiz.explanation: Each additional parallel path provides an extra route for current, lowering the equivalent resistance.

title: Bending Light: Reflection & Refraction
summary: Bend mirrors and lenses by hand to discover how reflection, refraction, and total internal reflection actually work.
theory: Light travels in straight lines until it meets a new surface, where it obeys one of two rules. **Reflection**: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; curving the mirror (concave) gathers parallel rays to a single **principal focus (F)**, related to the radius of curvature by f = R/2. **Refraction**: light changes speed crossing between media, bending its path according to Snell's Law, n = sin i / sin r. A convex lens uses this to focus light to a point whose position depends on the object distance u relative to f (1/v − 1/u = 1/f). When light inside a denser medium hits a boundary steeper than the **critical angle** (sin θc = 1/n), it undergoes **total internal reflection** and cannot escape at all — the principle behind optical fibres.

procedure.title: Bend the concave mirror
procedure.description: Drag the glowing ring on the mirror's rim to change its curvature and watch the focal point F move.

procedure.title: Find the burning point
procedure.description: Slide the paper screen until it sits exactly at F and observe what happens; then switch to bulb mode and place the bulb at F to produce a parallel beam.

procedure.title: Squash the convex lens
procedure.description: Drag the candle and the lens, and use the bulge handle to change the lens's focal length. Note how the image changes from real & inverted to virtual & magnified as the candle crosses F.

procedure.title: Find the critical angle
procedure.description: Drag the torch inside the glass/water/diamond block and sweep the angle until the beam suddenly stops escaping — that is the critical angle, and beyond it you get total internal reflection.

procedure.title: Build an instrument
procedure.description: On the optician's bench, arrange the two lenses and the object to complete each mission: a telescope, a microscope, and a projector.

observation: The mirror's focal length shortens as its curvature deepens, matching f = R/2. The lens image flips from real/inverted to virtual/magnified exactly when the object crosses the focal point. Total internal reflection begins abruptly once the incidence angle passes the critical angle predicted by sin θc = 1/n, with denser media (diamond) showing a much smaller critical angle than water or glass.

quiz.question: Bending a concave mirror to a deeper curve (smaller radius of curvature) will:

options.text: Move the focal point farther away
Move the focal point closer to the mirror

quiz.explanation: Since f = R/2, a smaller radius of curvature R produces a shorter focal length f, pulling the focus closer to the mirror.

quiz.question: A candle placed exactly at a convex lens's focal point produces:

options.text: No image — the outgoing rays are parallel

quiz.explanation: At u = f, the lens equation gives v = infinity: every ray leaves the lens parallel to the axis, so no image forms.

quiz.question: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels:

options.text: From a denser medium into a rarer medium, above the critical angle
From a rarer medium into a denser medium, at any angle

quiz.explanation: TIR requires light moving from higher to lower refractive index, and only once the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle sin θc = 1/n.

title: Acid-Base Titration
summary: Determine the concentration of an unknown acid by titrating it against a standard base.
theory: Titration is a volumetric technique used to determine the concentration of an analyte by reacting it with a titrant of known concentration. At the **equivalence point**, moles of acid equal moles of base, indicated by a colour change in the chosen indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein).

procedure.title: Prepare the burette
procedure.description: Fill the burette with standardized NaOH solution and record the initial reading.

procedure.title: Add indicator
procedure.description: Add 2-3 drops of phenolphthalein to the acid solution in the conical flask.

procedure.title: Titrate to the endpoint
procedure.description: Add base drop-wise while swirling until a persistent faint pink colour appears.

procedure.title: Calculate concentration
procedure.description: Use the titrant volume and the neutralization equation to compute the acid's molarity.

observation: The solution turns from colourless to a persistent light pink at the endpoint. Repeat titrations should agree within 0.1 mL (concordant readings).

quiz.question: At the equivalence point of a strong acid-strong base titration, the pH is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Strong acid-strong base neutralization produces a neutral salt solution, pH ≈ 7.

title: Observing Plant and Animal Cell Structure
summary: Use a virtual microscope to compare the structure of plant and animal cells.
theory: All cells share common features such as a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and genetic material, but plant cells additionally have a **cell wall**, **chloroplasts**, and a large central **vacuole**, which animal cells lack.

procedure.title: Load the onion cell slide
procedure.description: Select the prepared onion epidermis slide in the virtual microscope.

procedure.title: Identify structures
procedure.description: Label the cell wall, nucleus, and cytoplasm using the annotation tool.

procedure.title: Switch to the cheek cell slide
procedure.description: Repeat identification for the human cheek cell sample and note the differences.

observation: Plant cells appear as regular, brick-like shapes with a visible cell wall; animal cells are irregular in outline and lack a cell wall.

quiz.question: Which organelle is found in plant cells but not typical animal cells?
quiz.explanation: Chloroplasts, used for photosynthesis, are unique to plant (and some protist) cells.

title: Exploring Basic Logic Gates
summary: Build AND, OR, and NOT gates and verify their truth tables.
theory: Logic gates are the building blocks of digital circuits. **AND** outputs true only when all inputs are true, **OR** outputs true when at least one input is true, and **NOT** inverts its single input.

procedure.title: Wire an AND gate
procedure.description: Connect two switches to an AND gate and observe the output LED for all input combinations.

procedure.title: Wire an OR gate
procedure.description: Replace the AND gate with an OR gate and repeat the observations.

procedure.title: Wire a NOT gate
procedure.description: Connect a single switch through a NOT gate and observe the inverted output.

procedure.title: Complete the truth tables
procedure.description: Fill in the truth table for each gate based on your observations.

observation: The AND gate LED lights only when both switches are on; the OR gate LED lights when either switch is on; the NOT gate LED is always opposite the switch state.

quiz.question: An OR gate with both inputs LOW (0) outputs:
quiz.explanation: OR outputs 1 only when at least one input is 1; with both inputs 0 the output is 0.

title: Mechanical Advantage of a Lever
summary: Investigate how effort, load, and fulcrum position affect a lever's mechanical advantage.
theory: A lever's **mechanical advantage (MA)** is the ratio of load arm to effort arm distances from the fulcrum: MA = effort arm length / load arm length. Moving the fulcrum closer to the load increases MA, making it easier to lift heavy loads with less effort.

procedure.title: Set the fulcrum at the midpoint
procedure.description: Place the fulcrum at the centre of the lever and hang a fixed load.

procedure.title: Measure required effort
procedure.description: Increase the applied effort force until the lever balances; record the value.

procedure.title: Move the fulcrum
procedure.description: Shift the fulcrum closer to the load and repeat the effort measurement.

procedure.title: Calculate MA
procedure.description: Compute mechanical advantage for each fulcrum position and compare.

observation: As the fulcrum moves closer to the load, the effort required to balance the lever decreases, confirming that mechanical advantage increases.

quiz.question: Moving the fulcrum closer to the load will generally:

options.text: Reverse the direction of the load

quiz.explanation: A longer effort arm relative to the load arm increases mechanical advantage, reducing required effort.

title: Friction on an Inclined Plane
summary: Measure the coefficient of friction by sliding a block down inclined planes of varying angle.
theory: A block on an incline experiences gravity, a normal force, and friction. The block begins to slide when the component of gravity along the incline exceeds the maximum static friction force, giving **tan(θ) = μ_s** at the critical angle.

procedure.title: Set a shallow angle
procedure.description: Start with a low incline angle and place the block at the top.

procedure.title: Increase the angle gradually
procedure.description: Slowly raise the incline until the block just begins to slide; record this critical angle.

procedure.title: Repeat with different surfaces
procedure.description: Switch the block's surface material and repeat to compare friction coefficients.

procedure.title: Calculate μ_s
procedure.description: Use μ_s = tan(θ) to compute the coefficient of static friction for each surface.

observation: Rougher surfaces require a steeper critical angle before sliding begins, corresponding to a higher coefficient of static friction.

quiz.question: At the critical sliding angle θ, the coefficient of static friction μ_s equals:
quiz.explanation: At the point of sliding, gravity's component along the incline equals the maximum friction force, giving μ_s = tan(θ).

title: Graphing Linear Equations
summary: Visualize how slope and intercept shape the graph of y = mx + c.
theory: A linear equation in the form **y = mx + c** graphs as a straight line, where m is the slope (rate of change) and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). Changing m rotates the line; changing c shifts it vertically.

procedure.title: Set m = 1, c = 0
procedure.description: Plot the baseline y = x and observe the 45° line through the origin.

procedure.title: Vary the slope
procedure.description: Change m to different positive and negative values and observe the line's rotation.

procedure.title: Vary the intercept
procedure.description: Keep m fixed and change c, observing the vertical shift of the line.

observation: Increasing |m| makes the line steeper; a negative m flips its direction. Changing c translates the line up or down without altering its slope.

quiz.question: In y = mx + c, increasing c while keeping m constant will:
quiz.explanation: c is the y-intercept; changing it moves the line up or down while its slope stays the same.
